question: What proportion of females of childbearing potential are asked whether they are or might be pregnant before a diagnostic nuclear medicine radiopharmaceutical is administered?
why: No closed-loop audit of pregnancy enquiry before radiopharmaceutical administration has been published in the library, despite the department holding zero audits overall; the nearest related work covers pregnancy testing in emergency surgery, not nuclear medicine [7712][6008].

standard.source: Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017, regulation 11(1)(f); ARSAC Notes for Guidance on the Clinical Administration of Radiopharmaceuticals and Use of Sealed Radioactive Sources (January 2016), paragraph 7.3
standard.wording: a person must not carry out an exposure unless... in the case of an individual of childbearing potential, the person has enquired whether that individual is pregnant or breastfeeding, if relevant. [IR(ME)R reg 11(1)(f)] Any female of childbearing potential undergoing procedures involving radiopharmaceuticals should therefore be asked whether she is or might be pregnant. A policy should be established on the age range of females involved (eg 12 to 55 years) and followed unless there are known exceptional circumstances applying to an individual patient. [ARSAC 7.3]

population: Inclusion: all female patients aged 12-55 having a diagnostic radiopharmaceutical administration in the nuclear medicine department. Exclusion: males, females outside the age policy, therapy administrations (audited separately).
sample: 40 consecutive eligible female attendances over the last 2-3 months, from the nuclear medicine booking system.
data_source: Nuclear medicine request form and radiographer/technologist pre-administration checklist; RIS/PACS administration record.
change: Add a mandatory, hard-stop 'pregnancy/breastfeeding status' field to the electronic nuclear medicine request and the radiographer's pre-administration checklist for all females aged 12-55, which must be completed before the radiopharmaceutical can be released from the hot lab electronically.
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size, after the hard-stop field goes live.
close_loop: Present at the nuclear medicine/radiology governance meeting; if the target is met, keep the field mandatory in the RIS build specification so it survives system upgrades.
evidence: [7712] pregnancy testing in acute abdominal pain: 41.8% before intervention -> 80% after a teaching and poster intervention (nearest comparable pregnancy-status audit)
[6008] pregnancy status documented in emergency surgical admissions: 30% -> 75% after a clerking prompt (form change)
No nuclear medicine-specific pregnancy enquiry audit exists in the library
pitfalls: Staff assume the referring clinician already asked → make the nuclear medicine department's own record the audited item, not the referral letter.
Postmenopausal-looking patients are skipped without a documented reason → require the field for every patient in the age band regardless of appearance.
'Not applicable' is used as a default tick with no real enquiry → spot-check 10 records against the radiographer's verbal recollection where possible.
Emergency or inpatient scans bypass the checklist out of hours → include an out-of-hours pathway in the hard stop, not just outpatient bookings.
Gains fade when the checklist is a paper sticker that runs out → build the field into the RIS/hot lab release step so it cannot be skipped.
pearls: Recruit the ARSAC certificate holder and radiation protection supervisor as co-authors; they own the justification process.
Pair this with an audit of what happens after a positive or uncertain answer, to show the safety net works end to end.
Use the hot lab's own dispensing log as a ready-made sample frame.
Keep the field mandatory in any future RIS or EPR migration by writing it into the system specification, not just local policy.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from the RIS and nuclear medicine request forms
pass: A dated entry made before administration records that the patient was asked whether she is or might be pregnant, with the answer, for every female aged 12-55.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: Before administering a diagnostic radiopharmaceutical to a breastfeeding woman, what proportion of patients have documented advice on any need to interrupt breastfeeding and for how long?
why: Nuclear medicine has no audits at all in the library; breastfeeding advice after radiopharmaceutical administration is a recognised radiation-protection duty that is easy to miss under time pressure.

standard.source: ARSAC Notes for Guidance on the Clinical Administration of Radiopharmaceuticals and Use of Sealed Radioactive Sources (January 2016), Section 7, paragraph 7.8
standard.wording: Specific instructions must be given to the mother of an infant in order to minimise irradiation to the latter.

population: Inclusion: all breastfeeding women having a diagnostic radiopharmaceutical administration. Exclusion: therapy administrations (audited separately, see companion audit).
sample: All eligible cases over the last 12 months (expect 15-30 in most departments); identify from the nuclear medicine booking system 'breastfeeding' flag or free-text notes.
data_source: Nuclear medicine request form, pre-administration checklist, patient information leaflet given, RIS record.
change: Add a radiopharmaceutical-specific breastfeeding interruption table (built from the ARSAC appendix) to the department protocol, with a mandatory 'breastfeeding advice given: yes/no, duration' field in the pre-administration checklist and a matching printed patient leaflet.
close_loop: Present to the radiation protection committee; if achieved, add the table to the RIS order comments so it prints automatically on the patient information sheet.
evidence: No breastfeeding-advice audit for nuclear medicine exists in the library; nearest related work is general pregnancy-status documentation in emergency admissions [6008]
pitfalls: Small numbers make a single missed case swing the percentage sharply → report a running total across 12 months rather than a single quarter.
Staff give verbal-only advice with nothing written → count only advice that is documented, since undocumented advice cannot be checked later.
Interruption times vary between local guides and can be quoted inconsistently → agree one reference table with the radiation protection adviser before cycle 1.
Bottle-fed top-ups are missed when only 'breastfeeding: yes/no' is recorded → capture whether expressed milk in advance was discussed.
The checklist prompt is answered from memory without checking the table → require the specific duration to be written, not just 'advised'.
pearls: Recruit the radiation protection supervisor to build and maintain the interruption-time table.
Laminate the table at the hot lab dispensing point so staff use it in real time.
Audit alongside the pregnancy-enquiry audit using the same data collection visit.
Hand the finished table to the infant feeding team so ward staff give consistent advice too.
effort: ~15 min per patient from RIS and department records
pass: For every breastfeeding patient, the notes or discharge information record whether breastfeeding needs to be interrupted, and if so for how long, using the department's agreed radiopharmaceutical-specific interruption times.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of women given a therapeutic dose of a long-lived radionuclide (for example radioactive iodine-131 or strontium-89) have documented advice on the period for which they should avoid pregnancy?
why: No audit of contraception advice after radionuclide therapy exists in the library; the harm from a fetal exposure during this period is well described but the advice step is easy to omit in a busy therapy list.

standard.source: ARSAC Notes for Guidance on the Clinical Administration of Radiopharmaceuticals and Use of Sealed Radioactive Sources (January 2016), paragraphs 7.11-7.12 and Table 7.1
standard.wording: In some circumstances it will be necessary to advise females not to become pregnant for a period following the administration of long-lived radiopharmaceuticals. The female patient should be advised to avoid pregnancy for a period following therapy administration as given in Table 7.1.

population: Inclusion: all female patients of childbearing potential given a therapeutic radionuclide administration (e.g. I-131, Sr-89, Y-90). Exclusion: males, post-menopausal women with documented reason for exemption.
sample: All eligible cases over the last 12-18 months (expect 15-30 in a typical unit) from the ARSAC therapy administration log.
data_source: ARSAC therapy certificate administration record, nuclear medicine physician's clinic letter, patient discharge information.
change: Add the Table 7.1 avoid-pregnancy durations to the therapy consent form as a pre-printed line specific to each radionuclide, completed and signed as part of the consent discussion.
close_loop: Present to the nuclear medicine/oncology therapy governance meeting; if met, keep the durations on the consent form template used for every future therapy patient.
evidence: No radionuclide therapy contraception-advice audit exists in the library; nearest related nuclear medicine quality audit is myocardial perfusion imaging technique [3998]
pitfalls: Small therapy numbers make percentages unstable → report counts as well as percentages and extend the sample window if needed.
Advice is given verbally at a busy clinic and not written down → count only documented advice.
Different radionuclides have very different durations (0 to 24 months in Table 7.1) → check the duration against the correct nuclide and activity, not a single blanket figure.
Male patients are wrongly included → apply sex- and radionuclide-specific inclusion criteria strictly.
The consent form pre-printed line is not updated when ARSAC guidance changes → assign the radiation protection adviser to review the form annually.
pearls: Recruit the clinical oncologist or nuclear medicine physician who runs the therapy list as co-lead.
Combine data collection with the existing consent-form audit visit to save time.
Ask the ARSAC certificate holder to check the table wording used on the form before cycle 1.
Keep a laminated Table 7.1 summary in the therapy suite for quick reference.
effort: ~15 min per patient from the ARSAC therapy log
pass: The notes or a signed patient information sheet record the specific avoid-pregnancy period given for the radionuclide and activity used, matching the department's Table 7.1-based policy.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: Where a nuclear medicine referral is for a procedure resulting in a fetal dose that could exceed 1 mGy and pregnancy cannot be excluded, what proportion of cases have documented consideration of the justification by the ARSAC certificate holder in consultation with the responsible clinician?
why: This decision point protects the fetus in the highest-risk nuclear medicine scenario and has no audit anywhere in the library; the department currently holds no nuclear medicine audits at all.

standard.source: ARSAC Notes for Guidance on the Clinical Administration of Radiopharmaceuticals and Use of Sealed Radioactive Sources (January 2016), paragraphs 7.4-7.5
standard.wording: Where a patient is probably or definitely pregnant, the justification for the procedure should be considered by the ARSAC certificate holder following consultation with the clinician responsible for the patient... The principle adopted here is that the absorbed dose to a foetus should not exceed 1 mGy.

population: Inclusion: all nuclear medicine referrals in probably or definitely pregnant patients over the audit period. Exclusion: procedures with an estimated fetal dose below 1 mGy where a lower-tier justification applies.
sample: All eligible cases over the last 18-24 months (expect a small number, 5-15, in most departments); identify from the nuclear medicine incident log and booking system pregnancy flags.
data_source: Nuclear medicine referral, ARSAC certificate holder's clinical note, multidisciplinary discussion record.
change: Create a one-page 'pregnant patient nuclear medicine justification' proforma that the ARSAC certificate holder must complete and file before any such administration proceeds, replacing informal verbal sign-off.
reaudit: At 12 months given the small expected caseload, same template.
close_loop: Present at the radiation protection committee; embed the proforma as a mandatory step in the department's IR(ME)R employer procedures.
evidence: No comparable pregnant-patient nuclear medicine justification audit exists in the library
pitfalls: Very small numbers mean a single case can dominate the percentage → report as a narrative case review alongside the rate, and pool data over a longer period.
Verbal-only sign-off leaves no auditable trail → require the proforma to be filed in the patient record, not just discussed at handover.
Urgent out-of-hours requests bypass the process → give the on-call ARSAC deputy the same proforma and authority.
Dose estimates are looked up inconsistently → agree one reference dose table (ARSAC Appendix I) for all staff to use.
The audit is seen as too rare to matter → frame it as a never-event-equivalent check, since a missed fetal dose review is a serious incident.
pearls: Recruit the ARSAC certificate holder and radiation protection adviser together; both are needed to define 'probable pregnancy'.
Use any radiation incident or Datix reports from the same period as a cross-check for missed cases.
Keep the case log so future re-audits do not start from zero.
Report this as a standing item at the quarterly radiation safety committee even between formal audit cycles.
effort: ~30 min per case, using existing incident and booking records
pass: For every case where pregnancy is probable or confirmed and the standard fetal dose estimate for the requested study could exceed 1 mGy, the notes show the ARSAC certificate holder's documented justification decision made in consultation with the referring clinician before administration.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of nuclear medicine requests have a documented justification statement, recording the referrer's clinical information and the practitioner's net-benefit decision, before the radiopharmaceutical is administered?
why: Justification is the cornerstone of IR(ME)R but nuclear medicine has zero audits in the library, so there is no evidence this step is reliably documented rather than assumed.

standard.source: Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017, regulations 10(2), 10(5) and 11(1)(b)
standard.wording: A person must not carry out an exposure unless... it has been justified by the practitioner as showing a sufficient net benefit giving appropriate weight to the matters set out in paragraph (2) [reg 11(1)(b)]. The referrer must supply the practitioner with sufficient medical data... to enable the practitioner to decide whether there is a sufficient net benefit as required by regulation 11(1)(b) [reg 10(5)].

population: Inclusion: all nuclear medicine studies performed over the sample period. Exclusion: none.
sample: 40 consecutive studies over the last month, from the RIS worklist.
data_source: RIS request and authorisation record, referral letter.
change: Configure the RIS so a study cannot move to 'ready for administration' status until a named practitioner has completed a structured justification field, and reject referrals lacking minimum clinical information back to the referrer electronically.
close_loop: Present at the imaging governance meeting; if achieved, lock the RIS workflow change so it cannot be bypassed by new starters.
evidence: No nuclear medicine justification-documentation audit exists in the library; the nearest general imaging justification work concerns intravascular contrast media use [9190]
pitfalls: 'Justified' is ticked as a default without a real clinical review → spot-check a sample against the referral letter for evidence of genuine review.
Referrers give minimal clinical information and practitioners justify anyway under time pressure → track the proportion of referrals returned for more information as a balancing measure.
Locum or out-of-hours practitioners are unfamiliar with the workflow → include them explicitly in training before cycle 1.
The audit is seen as a paperwork exercise → link it explicitly to the IR(ME)R employer procedures the department must hold under regulation 6.
Gains fade after a RIS upgrade resets defaults → re-check the build after any system change.
pearls: Recruit the lead nuclear medicine physician and RIS administrator together.
Use the RIS audit trail (who authorised, when) rather than manual note review, to make data collection fast.
Present alongside the employer's regulation 7 clinical audit requirement so it counts towards statutory compliance.
Keep a simple one-page justification checklist at each workstation as a visual reminder.
effort: ~10 min per 10 studies from the RIS audit trail
pass: The RIS record shows a named practitioner's justification decision (accepted, modified or rejected) linked to the clinical information supplied by the referrer, dated before the administration.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: When a scan modality using ionising radiation and one not using ionising radiation would give equivalent diagnostic information and both are available in the required timeframe, what proportion of nuclear medicine referrals in females of childbearing potential record that the non-ionising alternative was considered?
why: ARSAC explicitly requires this comparison but no audit of it exists anywhere in the library, and nuclear medicine has no audits at all to build on.

standard.source: ARSAC Notes for Guidance on the Clinical Administration of Radiopharmaceuticals and Use of Sealed Radioactive Sources (January 2016), paragraph 3.12
standard.wording: Where two imaging investigations exist that give equivalent information and both are available to the patient within the timeframe of their clinical management, then on radiation protection grounds the investigation not utilising ionising radiation should be used.

population: Inclusion: nuclear medicine referrals in females aged 12-55 for indications with a recognised non-ionising alternative (e.g. hepatobiliary, renal, some cardiac indications). Exclusion: indications with no equivalent non-ionising test (e.g. bone scan for metastases, most oncology PET).
sample: 30-40 consecutive eligible referrals over the last 3-4 months, identified at vetting.
data_source: RIS vetting record, referral letter.
change: Add a vetting prompt 'is there an equivalent non-ionising test available in time?' to the RIS vetting screen for the defined indication list, requiring a documented reason if nuclear medicine proceeds anyway.
close_loop: Present at the imaging vetting governance meeting; embed the prompt list in the department's referral guidelines if it reduces avoidable ionising studies.
evidence: No audit of ARSAC 3.12 alternative-modality consideration exists in the library
pitfalls: Vetting radiologists disagree on which indications have a true equivalent → agree the indication list with nuclear medicine and radiology leads before cycle 1.
The prompt is answered reflexively without genuine review → sample-check against actual imaging availability that week.
Urgent cases are wrongly excluded by reviewers who assume urgency overrides the rule → clarify that urgency is a valid documented reason, not an exemption from documenting.
Small numbers for rarer indications → pool similar indications rather than analysing each separately.
The change is not kept once the auditor rotates → give ownership to the vetting radiologist rota, not one individual.
pearls: Recruit both a nuclear medicine physician and a radiologist who vets ultrasound/MRI requests.
Start with the highest-volume indication with a real alternative (e.g. some hepatobiliary or renal referrals) rather than trying to cover everything at once.
Track downstream outcomes (was the alternative test diagnostic?) as a simple balancing measure.
Share results with GPs/referrers to reduce inappropriate initial requests, not just at the vetting stage.
effort: ~15 min per 10 referrals from RIS vetting notes
pass: For referrals in females aged 12-55 where a non-ionising alternative (e.g. ultrasound or MRI) could answer the same clinical question within the required timeframe, the vetting practitioner's note records that this was considered.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of nuclear medicine reports flagged by the reporting physician as containing an unexpected significant finding unrelated to the clinical question have a documented fail-safe communication to the referring team within 24 hours?
why: Nuclear medicine holds no audits in the library despite reporting incidental findings (for example unexpected uptake suggesting malignancy on a bone or cardiac scan) that need the same fail-safe pathway as other imaging.

standard.source: Royal College of Radiologists, Standards for the communication of radiological reports and fail-safe alert notification (2016)
standard.wording: Critical and urgent findings: Where emergency action is required as soon as possible, or medical evaluation is required within 24 hours... Radiologist should inform verbally (by telephone) the appropriate referring clinician/team of an unexpected acute life- or limb-threatening finding which requires emergency clinical action. He/she should document that this was done, (when and to who) within the radiology report or via an addendum.

population: Inclusion: all nuclear medicine reports over the audit period coded or flagged by the reporting physician as containing an unexpected significant finding. Exclusion: findings that are the direct subject of the requested study.
sample: All flagged cases over the last 6-12 months (expect a small number in most departments; extend the window if fewer than 20 are found).
data_source: RIS/PACS flagged report list, fail-safe communication log.
change: Add a 'fail-safe alert' flag to the nuclear medicine reporting template that, when selected, opens a mandatory field for the name, role and time of the person notified, matching the RCR fail-safe categories.
close_loop: Present at the imaging governance meeting; keep the flag mandatory in the RIS reporting template if the target is met.
evidence: No fail-safe communication audit for nuclear medicine exists in the library; the RCR standard already underpins related imaging fail-safe audits for other modalities
pitfalls: Reporting physicians under-flag borderline findings to avoid extra work → agree explicit example cases with the department before cycle 1.
Manual telephone calls are not documented when busy → make documentation, not the call itself, the audited step, and stress both matter equally.
Small numbers make the percentage swing on one case → report counts as well as percentages.
Out-of-hours reporting (teleradiology) has a different communication pathway → check that pathway is covered by the same standard.
Once the flag is added, staff use it inconsistently between reporters → include the flag definition in reporter induction.
pearls: Recruit the lead nuclear medicine physician and PACS administrator to build the flag together.
Cross-check against the Datix/incident system for any delayed-communication incidents in the same period.
Share results with the wider imaging fail-safe alert audit so nuclear medicine is not reported separately from other modalities.
Keep a running log so this becomes a rolling rather than one-off measure, given the low case numbers.
effort: ~20 min per flagged case from RIS and communication logs
pass: For each report flagged as containing an unexpected significant finding, the report or an addendum documents that the referring team was informed, by whom, when and how (verbal call, electronic alert or both), within 24 hours of report verification.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of adult diagnostic nuclear medicine administrations use activities that are, on review, the minimum consistent with obtaining the required diagnostic information, as documented against the department's local diagnostic reference level for that study?
why: Optimisation of administered activity is a specific ARSAC and IR(ME)R duty, and nuclear medicine has no audits in the library to show whether local reference levels are actually reviewed and used.

standard.source: Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017, regulation 12 (Optimisation); ARSAC Notes for Guidance (January 2016), paragraph 3.11
standard.wording: In some cases, if the patient is healthy and cooperative, activity might be reduced and scan times increased... it is important that the diagnostic information produced is not compromised by reduction in activity.

population: Inclusion: all adult diagnostic nuclear medicine administrations of a defined, high-volume study type (for example bone scan or DMSA) over the audit period. Exclusion: paediatric and therapy administrations.
sample: 40 consecutive administrations of the chosen study type over the last 2-3 months, from the hot lab dispensing log.
data_source: Hot lab dispensing record, department local diagnostic reference level document.
change: Publish or update the department's local diagnostic reference levels for its highest-volume studies and build the expected activity range into the hot lab dispensing checklist so any deviation must be justified at the point of dispensing.
target: ≥95% within range or with a documented reason
reaudit: At 6 months, same study type and sample size.
close_loop: Present at the radiation protection committee; if achieved, submit the reviewed local diagnostic reference levels for medical physics expert sign-off and keep them under the department's regulation 13 population dose review.
evidence: No nuclear medicine activity-optimisation audit exists in the library
pitfalls: Activity is rounded up 'to be safe' without review → require the reason field to be completed whenever the range is exceeded, not just for underdosing.
Weight-banding is applied inconsistently between staff → agree one banding table before cycle 1.
Small numbers for less common studies → start with the highest-volume study type only.
The local diagnostic reference level itself may be outdated → check it was reviewed within the last 3 years as part of this audit.
Gains fade if the range is only in a policy document nobody reads → put it directly on the dispensing screen or log sheet.
pearls: Recruit the medical physics expert to confirm the local diagnostic reference levels used.
Compare local levels with the national diagnostic reference levels where published, as a sense check.
Use the hot lab's electronic dispensing log to pull data quickly rather than manual note review.
Report administered activity trends over time as a simple run chart at the radiation safety meeting.
effort: ~10 min per 10 administrations from the hot lab log
pass: The administered activity for each case is within the department's written local diagnostic reference level range for that study and patient size/weight band, or a documented clinical reason is given for exceeding it.

question: What proportion of full blood count, urea and electrolyte, and liver function test requests from the emergency department are reported and available to the requestor within 1 hour of the sample reaching the laboratory?
why: No audit of this specific RCPath key performance indicator for emergency biochemistry and haematology turnaround exists in the library.

standard.source: Royal College of Pathologists, Key Performance Indicators in Pathology (CEff 090413, version 4, final)
standard.wording: Percentage of renal function, liver function tests and full blood counts requested by A&E completed and available to the requestor within 1 hour of receipt including out-of-hours... Challenge: 99% within 12 hours by April 2012 and 99% within 8 hours by April 2014.

population: Inclusion: all FBC, U&E and LFT requests from the emergency department over the sample period, including out-of-hours. Exclusion: samples rejected for quality reasons (audited separately).
sample: 60 consecutive ED requests (20 of each test type) over the last 2 weeks, from the LIMS.
data_source: Laboratory information management system (LIMS) sample-received and result-verified timestamps.
change: Move ED FBC/U&E/LFT samples to a dedicated fast-track analyser lane with automated exception reporting for any sample not verified within 1 hour, flagged live to the duty biomedical scientist.
close_loop: Present at the pathology and ED joint governance meeting; keep the fast-track lane and exception report as standard if the target is met.
evidence: [8290] laboratory turnaround time: GP reports reaching destination within 1-2 days improved from 13%/68% to a faster courier-based service (nearest comparable turnaround audit)
No ED 1-hour biochemistry/haematology turnaround audit against this specific RCPath KPI exists in the library
pitfalls: 'Receipt' time is defined inconsistently (sample taken vs sample scanned into the lab) → fix one definition in writing before cycle 1.
Overnight staffing dips slow turnaround → report day and night separately.
Repeat or duplicate requests inflate the denominator → count unique clinical episodes, not every repeat.
Analyser downtime distorts one week's data → extend the sample window if an outage occurred.
Gains fade once the fast-track lane is deprioritised at busy times → make the exception report a standing agenda item, not a one-off fix.
pearls: Recruit the ED lead and the biomedical scientist in charge of the analyser floor together.
Use the LIMS exception report as an ongoing dashboard rather than manual timestamp pulling each cycle.
Share turnaround data at the ED's own quality meeting, since delays there drive breaches of the 4-hour target.
Keep a rolling 3-month view rather than a single-point audit, given daily variation.
effort: ~15 min per 10 samples from LIMS timestamps
pass: The laboratory information system timestamp shows the verified result available to the requestor within 1 hour of the sample being received in the laboratory.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of biochemistry, haematology, microbiology and virology results meeting the laboratory's agreed critical-result definitions are actively communicated (telephoned or otherwise directly notified) to the requesting clinical team within 2 hours of the result becoming available?
why: This overall cross-discipline RCPath key performance indicator for critical result communication has not been audited across all four disciplines together in the library; existing entries focus on single analytes.

standard.source: Royal College of Pathologists, Key Performance Indicators in Pathology (CEff 090413, version 4, final)
standard.wording: Percentage of biochemistry, haematology, medical microbiology and virology critical requests phoned/actively communicated by laboratory within 2 hours of result being available to the laboratory (includes out of hours)... Challenge: 90% by April 2012 increasing to 97% by April 2014.

population: Inclusion: all results meeting the laboratory's written critical-result list across biochemistry, haematology, microbiology and virology over the audit period. Exclusion: results generated for research or non-clinical purposes.
sample: 40 consecutive critical results (10 per discipline where possible) over the last month, from the LIMS critical-result log.
data_source: LIMS critical-result flag and communication log.
change: Set a LIMS timer on every result flagged against the critical-result list that escalates to the duty biomedical scientist if it is not marked 'communicated' within 90 minutes, with a defined out-of-hours contact route for each clinical area.
close_loop: Present at the pathology quality meeting; if achieved, keep the LIMS escalation timer as a permanent safety-net feature.
evidence: No cross-discipline critical-result communication audit against this RCPath KPI exists in the library; single-analyte examples (potassium) are proposed separately
pitfalls: Different disciplines define 'critical' differently → agree and publish one combined list before cycle 1.
Electronic release alone is wrongly counted as 'communicated' → define communication strictly as an active, direct contact.
Out-of-hours calls to a switchboard rather than a named clinician are hard to verify → require the recipient's name and role to be logged.
Repeated critical results in the same patient inflate the count → count the first critical result per admission per analyte unless a new episode occurs.
The escalation timer is muted when busy → review timer override logs monthly.
pearls: Recruit a biomedical scientist lead from each discipline so the definition list has buy-in across the whole laboratory.
Use the existing LIMS critical-result flag as the sample frame rather than manual case-finding.
Pair this audit with the out-of-hours GP reporting audit, since both use the same escalation pathway.
Report separately for in-hours and out-of-hours performance, as they usually differ.
effort: ~15 min per 10 flagged results from the LIMS
pass: The LIMS shows the critical result was actively communicated (phone call or equivalent direct notification, not just electronic release) within 2 hours, with the recipient's name and time recorded.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of diagnostic (non-excision) histopathology biopsies are reported, confirmed and electronically authorised within 7 calendar days of the biopsy being taken?
why: No audit against this specific RCPath key performance indicator for diagnostic biopsy turnaround exists in the library; the closest entries show much longer turnaround (median 35-44 days) [8233] with no re-audit reported.

standard.source: Royal College of Pathologists, Key Performance Indicators in Pathology (CEff 090413, version 4, final)
standard.wording: Percentage of all biopsy cases (excluding those requiring decalcification) reported, confirmed, electronically authorised and electronically available to the requestor within 7 calendar days of biopsy being taken... Challenge: 80% by April 2012 increasing to 90% by April 2014.

population: Inclusion: all diagnostic biopsy specimens (not excision biopsies) received by histopathology over the sample period, identified by SNOMED/SNOMED-CT procedure code. Exclusion: specimens requiring decalcification.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible biopsy cases over the last 4-6 weeks, from the LIMS.
data_source: LIMS specimen-received date, report-authorised date, procedure code.
change: Introduce a documented system to flag and manage outstanding diagnostic biopsy cases approaching day 5, with a named consultant reviewing the outstanding-case list weekly, and prioritise diagnostic biopsy cassette processing ahead of larger resection specimens.
reaudit: At 6 months, same specimen definition and sample size.
close_loop: Present at the cellular pathology quality meeting; embed the weekly outstanding-case review permanently if the target is sustained.
evidence: [8233] inflammatory dermatosis histopathology: only 5/43 (11.6%) reported within 7 days, mean 44.4 days, median 35 days, with no re-audit reported
[5151] method for auditing histopathology turnaround against clinicians' stated requirements (no percentage given)
pitfalls: Decalcified and reflex-test cases are wrongly included, understating performance → apply the exclusion strictly and record reflex-test cases separately.
'Biopsy date' is recorded inconsistently (theatre date vs receipt date) → define it as the date the biopsy was taken, not received.
Staff shortages or a single absent reporter skew short samples → extend the window if a locum gap occurred.
Gains fade once the outstanding-case review stops being weekly → keep it on a fixed governance meeting agenda.
SNOMED coding errors misclassify excision biopsies as diagnostic biopsies → spot-check the procedure codes against the request form.
pearls: Recruit the cellular pathology clinical lead and a biomedical scientist who manages cut-up allocation.
Use the LIMS turnaround report rather than manual date extraction to make re-audit quick.
Share the outstanding-case list at the weekly departmental meeting, not just at audit time.
Track the proportion needing reflex tests separately, since these legitimately take longer and should not be blamed on the core process.
effort: ~10 min per 10 cases from the LIMS turnaround report
pass: The LIMS shows the diagnostic biopsy report (needle core, endoscopic, colposcopic or punch biopsy, excluding decalcified specimens) authorised within 7 calendar days of the biopsy date.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of all histopathology and diagnostic cytology cases (excluding those requiring decalcification) are reported, confirmed and electronically authorised within 10 calendar days of resection or procedure?
why: No audit against this overall RCPath turnaround key performance indicator exists in the library, separate from the narrower diagnostic-biopsy indicator.

standard.source: Royal College of Pathologists, Key Performance Indicators in Pathology (CEff 090413, version 4, final)
standard.wording: Percentage of all histopathology (excluding those requiring decalcification) and diagnostic cytology cases reported, confirmed, electronically authorised and electronically available to the requestor within 10 calendar days of resection or procedure... Challenge: 80% by April 2012 increasing to 90% by April 2014.

population: Inclusion: all histopathology resection specimens and diagnostic cytology cases over the sample period. Exclusion: decalcified specimens and cases covered by the separate 7-day diagnostic biopsy indicator.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible cases over the last 4-6 weeks, from the LIMS.
data_source: LIMS procedure date and report-authorised date.
change: Set up a documented, monitored system for prospective identification of outstanding cases (per RCPath KPI ix) so that any case unreported beyond the expected time is flagged and actioned, with exception reporting for cases still unreported after 20 calendar days.
reaudit: At 6 months, same specimen definition and sample size.
close_loop: Present at the cellular pathology and cancer MDT governance meeting; if met, keep the outstanding-case monitoring system as standard practice.
evidence: [8233] a related histopathology reporting audit found only 11.6% within 7 days for diagnostic biopsies, indicating turnaround is likely to be a live problem for overall reporting too
pitfalls: Major cancer resections needing multiple reflex tests are penalised unfairly → report cancer resections and benign resections separately.
'Procedure date' definitions differ between theatre and pathology systems → agree one source of truth before cycle 1.
A backlog from staff leave distorts a single sample window → extend the audit period if cover was reduced.
Gains fade once the exception report for 20-day-plus cases is not reviewed → assign a named consultant to review it weekly.
Integrated haematological malignancy reports needing multidisciplinary input may need a separate, longer target → agree this exclusion explicitly.
pearls: Recruit the cellular pathology lead and MDT coordinator, since delayed reports directly affect cancer MDT timelines.
Use the same LIMS report as the 7-day diagnostic biopsy audit, run for a different case set, to save data collection time.
Report the proportion of cases still outstanding beyond 20 days as a headline safety metric alongside the main percentage.
Track any downstream MDT delay caused by late reports as a balancing measure.
effort: ~10 min per 10 cases from the LIMS turnaround report
pass: The LIMS shows the report authorised within 10 calendar days of the resection or procedure date, for non-decalcified specimens.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of authorised histopathology reports use SNOMED or SNOMED-CT procedure, topography and morphology codes rather than free text?
why: No audit of pathology report coding completeness exists in the library, even though this RCPath key performance indicator underpins cancer registration, national audits and case-finding for other pathology KPIs.

standard.source: Royal College of Pathologists, Key Performance Indicators in Pathology (CEff 090413, version 4, final)
standard.wording: Challenge: 95% SNOMED or SNOMED-CT T, M and P codes by April 2012, 100% SNOMED OR SNOMED-CT T, M and P codes by April 2014.

population: Inclusion: all histopathology reports authorised over the sample period. Exclusion: none.
sample: 50 consecutive reports over the last 2 weeks, from the LIMS.
data_source: LIMS coding fields.
change: Make all three SNOMED code fields mandatory before a report can be electronically authorised in the LIMS, with a picklist rather than free text to reduce coding errors.
close_loop: Present at the cellular pathology quality meeting; if met, keep the mandatory coding fields switched on permanently, since they also support other KPIs and cancer registration.
evidence: No SNOMED coding-completeness audit exists in the library
pitfalls: Coding is completed but with the wrong code (miscoding) rather than missing entirely → this audit measures completeness only; pair with a separate coding-accuracy spot check if resources allow.
Legacy reports migrated from an old LIMS may lack codes and skew a retrospective sample → restrict the sample to reports authorised after the current LIMS went live.
Coders default to a generic code to satisfy the mandatory field → monitor for a spike in one non-specific code after the change.
Rare specimen types may lack a specific SNOMED code → agree a documented fallback process with the coding team.
The mandatory-field change is reversed during a system upgrade → re-check after every LIMS update.
pearls: Recruit the LIMS administrator and a biomedical scientist responsible for coding.
This is a quick, high-yield audit since it needs no manual clinical judgement, only a data extract.
Present the result alongside cancer registration data quality, since coding gaps affect national cancer statistics.
Use the audit as a trigger to refresh coding training for new starters.
effort: ~5 min per 10 reports from a LIMS data extract
pass: The authorised report carries a complete SNOMED or SNOMED-CT topography, morphology and procedure code set in the LIMS coding field.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of histopathology cases remaining unreported beyond 20 calendar days are identified and actioned through the department's exception-reporting system?
why: No audit of outstanding-case exception reporting exists in the library, even though RCPath specifically requires a documented system for this as a safety net beyond the routine turnaround KPIs.

standard.source: Royal College of Pathologists, Key Performance Indicators in Pathology (CEff 090413, version 4, final)
standard.wording: Each histopathology service is to have a documented system to identify cases remaining unreported longer than is anticipated, and to have a documented system to manage and report these cases. Exception reporting should be undertaken of all cases (including decalcified cases) remaining unreported after 20 calendar days.

population: Inclusion: all histopathology cases (including decalcified cases) received over the audit period that remain unreported at 20 calendar days. Exclusion: none.
sample: All such cases over the last 3 months (typically a small number; extend the window if fewer than 15 are found).
data_source: LIMS outstanding-case report, departmental exception log.
change: Set the LIMS to generate an automatic 20-day outstanding-case report every week, sent to a named consultant and the laboratory manager, with a required reason and action field for every case on it.
close_loop: Present at the cellular pathology quality meeting; keep the automatic weekly report running permanently if it is being acted on.
evidence: No outstanding-case exception-reporting audit exists in the library
pitfalls: Cases are removed from the outstanding list once reported without recording why they were late → require the reason to be logged before removal.
The report is generated but nobody is assigned to act on it → name an individual, not a team, as owner.
Reflex or referred-out cases dominate the list for legitimate reasons → record these separately from avoidable delays.
Small numbers make month-to-month variation look dramatic → track a rolling quarterly total.
The automatic report duplicates other workload lists and is ignored → integrate it into the single laboratory manager's daily dashboard rather than a separate email.
pearls: Recruit the laboratory manager and a consultant histopathologist as joint owners.
Use this audit to also surface any capacity or staffing gaps driving the delays, not just to check the paperwork exists.
Report the commonest reasons for delay to help target the fix (for example, a single bottleneck reporter or a specific reflex test).
Keep the exception log as a standing item at the departmental meeting even between formal audit cycles.
effort: ~20 min per month reviewing the exception log
pass: Every case still unreported at day 20 appears on a documented exception report, with a recorded reason and a named action or escalation.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of adults presenting with suspected acute coronary syndrome and managed on a high-sensitivity troponin early rule-out pathway have their second troponin sample taken at 3 hours (plus or minus 30 minutes) after the first, as the pathway specifies?
why: No audit of adherence to the specific NICE-recommended high-sensitivity troponin sampling interval exists in the library; related audits cover 6-month risk scoring and HbA1c testing after ACS, not the troponin timing protocol itself [in NNA-383/385].

standard.source: NICE Diagnostics Guidance DG15, Myocardial infarction (acute): early rule out using high-sensitivity troponin tests (October 2014)
standard.wording: The Elecsys Troponin T high-sensitive and ARCHITECT STAT High Sensitive Troponin-I assays are recommended as options for exclusion of non-ST-segment-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) in people presenting to an emergency department with chest pain and suspected acute coronary syndrome, when used with early-rule out protocols.

population: Inclusion: all adults presenting to the emergency department with suspected ACS placed on the high-sensitivity troponin early rule-out pathway over the sample period. Exclusion: patients with an obvious STEMI bypassing the pathway.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible ED patients over the last month, from the ED chest pain pathway log.
data_source: LIMS sample-collection timestamps, ED electronic chest pain pathway record.
change: Build an automatic timed reminder into the ED electronic chest pain pathway that alerts nursing staff when the second troponin is due, and flags on the results screen if it falls outside the 2.5-3.5 hour window.
close_loop: Present at the ED and cardiology joint governance meeting; keep the automatic reminder live if the target is met.
evidence: No audit of troponin sampling-interval protocol adherence exists in the library; related work covers post-diagnosis GRACE scoring and HbA1c testing after ACS, not the sampling protocol itself
pitfalls: ED overcrowding delays the second sample beyond the window → report separately for high-occupancy and normal-occupancy shifts.
Nursing handover loses track of the due time → the electronic reminder should persist across shift changes, not reset.
Patients who leave before the second sample are miscounted as protocol failures → record 'left before due' as a separate outcome.
Point-of-care and laboratory troponin results are mixed inconsistently → specify which assay platform counts for this pathway.
The reminder is silenced when the ED is busy → review alert-override logs periodically.
pearls: Recruit the ED chest pain pathway lead and a biomedical scientist from the biochemistry laboratory.
Use the ED electronic whiteboard's existing timers if one exists, rather than building a new system from scratch.
Report the proportion of patients successfully ruled out at 3 hours as a related outcome measure, to show the benefit of protocol adherence.
Keep the audit result visible on the ED results board so staff see their own performance in real time.
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from LIMS and ED pathway timestamps
pass: For every patient on the pathway, the second troponin sample is drawn between 2.5 and 3.5 hours after the first, as timestamped by the laboratory information system.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of samples sent to the laboratory are rejected because the patient identifiers on the sample do not match, or are missing from, the request?
why: No audit of overall sample-labelling rejection rate exists in the library, despite this being the single most common preventable cause of transfusion and other laboratory sample rejection nationally.

standard.source: Royal College of Pathologists, Key Performance Indicators in Pathology (CEff 090413, version 4, final), item viii Primary identifier
standard.wording: The NHS number or in Scotland the Community Health Index (CHI) to be used as the primary identifier.

population: Inclusion: all samples received by the core laboratory (biochemistry, haematology, microbiology) over the sample period. Exclusion: samples from services with a separate, already-audited labelling standard (for example transfusion, audited nationally).
sample: All rejected samples over the last month, plus a denominator of total samples received in the same period, from the LIMS rejection log.
data_source: LIMS sample-rejection log and total accession count.
change: Introduce point-of-collection barcode or electronic positive-patient-identification labelling in the two clinical areas generating the most labelling rejections, so labels are printed and applied at the bedside as a single continuous step.
target: Rejection rate below 1% of samples received
close_loop: Present at the pathology and nursing/phlebotomy joint governance meeting; expand electronic labelling to further wards if the pilot areas show a sustained fall.
evidence: [7693] transfusion sample mislabelling and wrong blood in tube: rejection rate rose from 2.99% to 4.4% between the 2012 and 2022 national comparative audits despite more sites introducing bedside electronic labelling (23% of sites, up 224%)
pitfalls: Rejection reasons are recorded inconsistently between shifts → agree one coded reason list before cycle 1.
Areas with the highest rejection rates resist being singled out → present rates by ward without individual staff names to keep the focus on the system.
A resampling delay from a rejected sample can itself cause harm (for example delayed antibiotics) → track this delay as a balancing measure.
Electronic labelling pilots stall without dedicated project support → assign a named implementation lead before starting.
Gains fade once new staff are not trained on the labelling process → include it in ward induction.
pearls: Recruit a biomedical scientist and a ward sister from the pilot area together.
Use the national transfusion comparative audit findings [7693] to show this is a recognised, worsening national problem, which helps secure support for change.
Report the resampling delay in hours as a tangible harm measure alongside the rejection rate.
Keep the barcode/electronic labelling pilot data live on a ward dashboard to sustain engagement.
effort: ~15 min per week from the LIMS rejection log
pass: Every sample accepted by the laboratory carries the patient's NHS number (or CHI in Scotland) along with name and date of birth, matching the request form exactly; any mismatch results in rejection and a logged reason.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of adult inpatients have the same blood test (full blood count or urea and electrolytes) requested and performed twice within a 24-hour period without a new clinical indication documented?
why: No audit of unnecessary duplicate ward blood test ordering exists in the library; related work shows unnecessary preoperative testing is common and responds well to a simple system change [7076][6456].

standard.source: Local standard, informed by NICE guideline NG45 on routine preoperative tests for elective surgery and Choosing Wisely UK principles on avoiding unnecessary repeat testing
standard.wording: Local standard: a repeat full blood count or urea and electrolytes test within 24 hours of a normal or unchanged previous result should have a documented new clinical indication (for example a change in condition, a new treatment started, or a scheduled monitoring protocol).

population: Inclusion: adult general medical or surgical inpatients with two or more requests for the same FBC or U&E panel within a 24-hour period. Exclusion: patients on a recognised monitoring protocol requiring daily or more frequent testing (e.g. acute kidney injury, electrolyte replacement).
sample: 40 consecutive eligible duplicate-test episodes over the last month, identified from the LIMS by matching patient and test type within 24 hours.
data_source: LIMS request history, medical and nursing notes.
change: Add a soft-stop alert to the electronic ordering system that flags when the same test has been requested within the last 24 hours and asks the ordering clinician to confirm the reason before the request is submitted.
target: ≥85% of repeats with a documented reason (equivalently, ≤15% unexplained duplicate requests)
close_loop: Present at the medical directorate quality meeting; if repeats fall, report the laboratory cost and phlebotomy time saved to sustain support for the alert.
evidence: [7076] routine preoperative blood tests for elective breast surgery: education and a poster cut inappropriate tests and produced a 71% reduction in spend
[6456] reducing unnecessary liver function tests on the paediatric intensive care unit (related unnecessary-testing audit, different population)
pitfalls: Genuine monitoring protocols (e.g. daily U&E on IV fluids) are wrongly flagged as unnecessary duplicates → build an explicit exclusion list before cycle 1.
Junior doctors order repeats defensively out of habit → pair the alert with a short teaching session on when repeat testing adds value.
The soft-stop is clicked through without real thought → sample-check a subset of overridden alerts for a genuine reason.
Reducing tests could delay detection of real deterioration → monitor a balancing measure such as unplanned escalations to ensure safety is not compromised.
Savings are hard to attribute without a clear baseline → record baseline test volume and cost before the alert goes live.
pearls: Recruit a biochemistry or haematology lead and a ward-based junior doctor educational supervisor.
Present the laboratory cost per avoided test as a concrete number for the business case.
Use existing LIMS request-pattern reports rather than manual note review to identify duplicate episodes quickly.
Share results with the trust's phlebotomy service, since fewer unnecessary requests reduce patient venepuncture burden too.
effort: ~15 min per 10 duplicate episodes from the LIMS and notes
pass: Where the same test is repeated within 24 hours, the request or notes record a specific new clinical reason (deterioration, new treatment, scheduled protocol); a repeat with no reason documented fails.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of unexpected malignant findings identified by pathology from a specimen taken for a benign or unrelated indication are actively flagged to the requesting clinician by telephone or an equivalent direct alert, in addition to the standard report?
why: No audit specifically of the active flagging step (as opposed to the eventual clinical action) for unexpected malignancy exists in the library; the corpus entry on this topic measures action within 14 days of the report, not whether an active alert was sent at the time of reporting [NNA-264].

standard.source: Royal College of Radiologists, Standards for the communication of radiological reports and fail-safe alert notification (2016)
standard.wording: Local policies of the referring institution will also define the need to send fail-safe alerts, for example, where there is a suspected but unexpected cancer on imaging... Significant, important, unexpected and actionable findings: Cases where the reporting radiologist feels that the findings are important and a fail-safe alert should be added to the normal communication method to ensure that they are acted upon in a timely manner.

population: Inclusion: all pathology and imaging reports over the audit period coded as containing an unexpected malignant finding unrelated to the original clinical question. Exclusion: findings that are the expected subject of the request (e.g. a cancer resection specimen).
sample: All eligible cases over the last 6 months (expect a small number; extend the window if fewer than 20 are found).
data_source: LIMS/RIS unexpected-finding flag, fail-safe communication log.
change: Add a mandatory 'unexpected malignancy - fail-safe alert sent' field, with recipient name, role and time, to the LIMS/RIS reporting template whenever the unexpected-finding code is used.
close_loop: Present at the joint pathology/radiology/MDT governance meeting; keep the mandatory field permanently if it is being reliably completed.
evidence: No audit of the active fail-safe alerting step (distinct from downstream action) for unexpected malignancy exists in the library
pitfalls: Reporters assume the standard report is enough and skip the extra alert → make the extra step explicit and separately auditable.
Small numbers make percentages swing on one case → report a running total across the audit period.
The alert is sent but not documented → count only documented alerts, since undocumented ones cannot be relied on later.
Weekend and out-of-hours cases have a different, less reliable alerting pathway → check this specifically as a sub-group.
Teams push back that this duplicates the MDT listing process → clarify that the alert is the immediate safety net, separate from and faster than the next MDT.
pearls: Recruit both a pathologist and a radiologist, since unexpected malignancy can arise from either specialty.
Cross-check against the MDT tracking list to find any cases that were never alerted at all.
Use this audit as a template for other 'significant, important, unexpected and actionable' findings beyond malignancy.
Report the time from authorisation to alert as well as whether an alert happened, to show speed as well as completeness.
effort: ~20 min per case from LIMS/RIS and communication logs
pass: For every pathology or imaging report containing an unexpected malignant finding unrelated to the requested indication, a fail-safe alert (telephone call, electronic flag or equivalent) is documented as sent, separate from the routine report, on the day of authorisation.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: Of positive blood cultures that grow after a patient has already been discharged from hospital, what proportion are telephoned within 2 hours of the result becoming available to a named clinician in the last team that cared for the patient?
why: No audit of post-discharge positive blood culture communication timeliness exists in the library, even though this is a recognised patient-safety gap distinct from the pre-discharge critical-result pathway.

standard.source: Royal College of Pathologists, Key Performance Indicators in Pathology (CEff 090413, version 4, final)
standard.wording: Percentage of biochemistry, haematology, medical microbiology and virology critical requests phoned/actively communicated by laboratory within 2 hours of result being available to the laboratory (includes out of hours)... Local agreements must be in place to cover patient pathways defining critical results and providing clear lines of communication and failsafe systems.

population: Inclusion: all blood cultures that flag positive after the patient's discharge date over the audit period. Exclusion: contaminants agreed as not clinically significant by the reporting microbiologist.
sample: All eligible cases over the last 3 months (expect a small but important number in most trusts).
data_source: Microbiology LIMS positive-culture flag, on-call communication log.
change: Add a 'patient discharged' flag to the microbiology LIMS positive-culture screen that automatically shows the last ward and the agreed emergency contact route (ED results clinician or ward team bleep), so the on-call biomedical scientist does not need to search manually.
close_loop: Present at the microbiology and acute medicine joint governance meeting; keep the automatic flag permanently if the target is met.
evidence: No post-discharge positive blood culture communication audit exists in the library; related work on blood cultures covers pre-discharge use in pyrexial surgical patients [1975]
pitfalls: The patient's GP is contacted instead of a hospital clinician with no documented handover of responsibility → require a named hospital clinician contact as the primary route, with GP notification as a secondary step.
Contact details for the discharging team are out of date → build the flag from the live bed management system, not a static ward list.
Small numbers make a single missed case very visible → use this as a positive, since even one miss should trigger a review.
Weekend discharges create a longer gap before someone reads the flag → check weekday/weekend performance separately.
Staff assume 'it will be picked up at GP follow-up' → make clear the 2-hour standard applies regardless of onward care plans.
pearls: Recruit the microbiology on-call lead and the acute medicine discharge team.
Use the existing critical-result LIMS infrastructure as the base and add the discharge-specific flag on top, rather than building something new.
Report each case as a mini case review at the microbiology governance meeting, given the low numbers and high stakes.
Share results with the ED, since it often becomes the default contact point for discharged patients.
effort: ~15 min per case from LIMS and on-call logs
pass: For each positive blood culture that turns positive after discharge, the microbiology on-call record shows a named clinician contacted by telephone within 2 hours, with the patient's last ward or team and the contact route documented.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of out-of-hours laboratory results requiring urgent clinical action are successfully communicated to primary care before the practice next opens?
why: No audit of out-of-hours critical-result communication specifically to primary care (as opposed to hospital teams) exists in the library.

standard.source: Royal College of Pathologists, Key Performance Indicators in Pathology (CEff 090413, version 4, final), guidance reference: Out-of-hours reporting of laboratory results requiring urgent clinical action to primary care: Advice to pathologists and those that work in laboratory medicine (RCPath, 2010)
standard.wording: Out-of-hours reporting of laboratory results requiring urgent clinical action to primary care: Advice to pathologists and those that work in laboratory medicine, The Royal College of Pathologists, 2010.

population: Inclusion: all GP-requested critical results generated out of hours (evenings, nights, weekends) over the sample period. Exclusion: results on hospital inpatients, audited under the hospital critical-result pathway.
sample: All eligible cases over the last 2-3 months (expect a modest number; extend the window if fewer than 20 are found).
data_source: LIMS out-of-hours critical-result log, GP communication record.
change: Agree a single, published out-of-hours contact route (a named number covering the local out-of-hours GP service) with primary care commissioners, and make it the default option on the LIMS critical-result communication screen for GP-requested tests.
close_loop: Present jointly at the laboratory governance meeting and the primary care/CCG-equivalent quality meeting; keep the agreed contact route live and review it annually.
evidence: No out-of-hours primary care critical-result communication audit exists in the library
pitfalls: GP practice contact numbers on requests are out of date → validate contact details against a current practice directory rather than the request form alone.
Out-of-hours GP services change provider without the laboratory being told → build a review of the contact route into the annual service review.
Small numbers make a single failure look large → report cumulatively over a longer period.
Biomedical scientists are unsure whom to call and default to 'no action' → give a clear escalation script and contact list at each workstation.
Gains fade if the agreed number is not kept up to date after staff turnover → assign ownership to a named laboratory manager.
pearls: Recruit a GP with an interest in patient safety, plus the laboratory out-of-hours lead, as joint authors.
Use this audit to formalise a route that may currently be informal or ad hoc.
Share results at a primary care network or locality meeting, since GPs are the direct beneficiaries.
Keep a simple laminated escalation card at the out-of-hours bench with the current contact numbers.
effort: ~15 min per case from LIMS and communication logs
pass: For every GP-requested result meeting the local critical-result list generated out of hours, the LIMS shows a documented, successful communication route to the GP practice (or the out-of-hours GP service) before the practice's next opening time.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of babies referred after newborn hearing screening are offered their first audiological assessment appointment within 4 weeks of the screening outcome (or by the corrected equivalent age if born prematurely)?
why: No audit of the national newborn hearing screening referral-to-appointment-offered standard exists in the library; related entries cover overall screening coverage [4934] and the diagnosis-to-ENT-review pathway after diagnosis [7944], not this specific step.

standard.source: NHS Newborn Hearing Screening Programme, Newborn hearing screening programme standards (NHSP-S04)
standard.wording: NHSP-S04: time from screening outcome to first offered appointment for audiological assessment. Babies should be offered first appointments within less than 4 weeks (28 days), or corrected age if born prematurely. Acceptable level: greater than or equal to 97.0%; achievable level: greater than or equal to 99.0%.

population: Inclusion: all babies referred for audiological assessment following newborn hearing screening over the sample period. Exclusion: babies referred through other routes (e.g. parental concern outside the screening programme).
sample: 40 consecutive eligible referrals over the last 3 months, from the child health/screening IT system and audiology booking system.
data_source: Newborn hearing screening programme IT system, audiology appointment booking system.
change: Set the newborn hearing screening IT system to automatically generate the audiology assessment referral and a suggested appointment slot at the point the screening outcome is recorded, rather than relying on a separate manual referral step.
close_loop: Present at the newborn hearing screening programme's quarterly quality assurance meeting; report against the national NHSP-S04 standard so results feed the mandatory national return.
evidence: [4934] post-newborn hearing surveillance programme coverage audit: 64.7-78.1% coverage against an 80% local benchmark (a related but different screening-pathway measure)

[7944] permanent childhood hearing impairment pathway redesign: mean diagnosis to first ENT review cut from 439.4 to 188.1 days with a new streamlined protocol (downstream pathway, not the initial referral-to-offer step)
pitfalls: Corrected age calculations for premature babies are done inconsistently → agree one calculation method with the screening programme lead before cycle 1.
Referrals lost between screening and audiology booking are not captured if only the booking system is checked → cross-reference both systems.

Cancelled or DNA'd first appointments are wrongly counted as 'offered on time' when the substantive assessment is delayed → record the offered date, not the attended date, for this specific standard (attendance is a separate standard, NHSP-S05).
Small caseloads at low-referral sites make monthly rates volatile → report quarterly.
Data quality issues in the national IT system are blamed for local delays → validate a sample manually against paper or local records.
pearls: Recruit the newborn hearing screening coordinator and audiology booking lead together.
This maps directly onto the mandatory national NHSP data return, so the audit produces data staff already need to submit.
Track NHSP-S05 (attendance within 4 weeks) alongside this as a natural companion audit.
Share results with maternity and health visiting teams, since delayed screening outcome communication upstream can also cause the referral to be offered late.
effort: ~10 min per 10 referrals from the screening and booking systems
pass: The audiology booking system shows a first assessment appointment offered within 28 days of the screening outcome date, or by the equivalent corrected age for babies born prematurely.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of babies referred after newborn hearing screening actually attend their audiological assessment appointment within 4 weeks of the screening outcome (or by the corrected equivalent age if born prematurely)?
why: No audit of the national newborn hearing screening attendance standard exists in the library; this measures a different step from the appointment-offered standard, since offering an appointment on time does not guarantee attendance.

standard.source: NHS Newborn Hearing Screening Programme, Newborn hearing screening programme standards (NHSP-S05)
standard.wording: NHSP-S05: time from screening outcome to attendance at an audiological assessment appointment. Babies should attend appointments within less than 4 weeks (28 days), or corrected age if born prematurely. Acceptable level: greater than or equal to 90.0%; achievable level: greater than or equal to 95.0%.

population: Inclusion: all babies referred for audiological assessment following newborn hearing screening over the sample period. Exclusion: babies referred through other routes outside the screening programme.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible referrals over the last 3 months, from the audiology booking and attendance system.
data_source: Audiology appointment attendance record, newborn hearing screening programme IT system.
change: Introduce a structured DNA-recovery process: any family who does not attend the first offered appointment is telephoned within 48 hours and offered a new slot within the remaining part of the 28-day window, rather than waiting for the next routine recall letter.
close_loop: Present at the newborn hearing screening quarterly quality assurance meeting alongside the NHSP-S04 result, and report against the national standard.
evidence: No attendance-specific audit against NHSP-S05 exists in the library; the companion offer-timeliness audit (NHSP-S04) is the nearest related measure
pitfalls: Families who move or change contact details between screening and the appointment are hard to trace, inflating apparent DNA rates → cross-check against the child health information system for a current address before counting a DNA.
Interpreter needs are not flagged at booking, leading to avoidable non-attendance → record whether an interpreter was booked when needed.
Transport or distance to the audiology clinic is a common but unrecorded barrier → add a free-text reason field for non-attendance.
Rebooked appointments outside the 28-day window are still recorded as 'attended' without flagging the delay → capture both dates in the template.
Gains fade if the 48-hour DNA callback is only done when staff have spare capacity → make it a defined task on the audiology admin rota.
pearls: Recruit an audiology administrator who manages DNAs day to day as co-author.
Use health visitor contacts as an additional route to encourage attendance for families who are hard to reach by phone.
Report DNA reasons thematically to target the fix (for example, transport support for families without a car).
Share the combined NHSP-S04/S05 results with the regional newborn hearing screening quality assurance coordinator, since these feed national reporting.
effort: ~10 min per 10 referrals from the audiology system
pass: The audiology system shows attendance at the assessment appointment within 28 days of the screening outcome date, or by the equivalent corrected age.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of adults assessed in routine adult hearing aid audiology clinics with sudden or rapid sensorineural hearing loss (a drop of more than 30 dB across at least three adjacent audiometric frequencies within 72 hours, or rapid progressive loss) are referred the same day for urgent medical assessment rather than continued on the routine pathway?
why: No audit exists in the library of whether audiology staff correctly identify and fast-track this specific non-routine presentation using the defined clinical criteria, as distinct from the ENT-side referral-to-treatment time audits already in the corpus.

standard.source: British Academy of Audiology, Guidance on Identifying Non-Routine Cases of Hearing Loss in Adults (April 2015)
standard.wording: Sudden or rapid hearing loss: Either a greater than 30 dB deterioration in sensorineural hearing loss occurring in at least three adjacent audiometric frequencies over 72 hours or less, or rapid onset of hearing loss or rapid deterioration in hearing.

population: Inclusion: all adults assessed in routine adult audiology clinics whose audiogram and history meet the BAA sudden/rapid hearing loss definition over the sample period. Exclusion: patients already under active ENT follow-up for the same episode.
sample: All eligible cases identified over the last 6-12 months (expect a small number; extend the window if fewer than 15 are found), cross-checked against clinic audiograms flagged for a sudden asymmetric or rapid change.
data_source: Audiology clinic record, audiogram comparison with any prior test, referral letter.
change: Add the BAA sudden/rapid hearing loss criteria as a mandatory check to the audiology assessment template, with an automatic same-day referral pathway (a single agreed phone number or e-referral route) triggered whenever the criteria are met.
close_loop: Present at the audiology and ENT joint governance meeting; keep the mandatory check and referral pathway live if the target is sustained.
evidence: No audit of audiology-side identification of sudden/rapid hearing loss against this BAA definition exists in the library; related ENT-side pathway audits measure time from referral to steroid treatment once the diagnosis is already made
pitfalls: Audiologists are unfamiliar with the precise BAA numerical definition and under- or over-refer → include worked examples in training before cycle 1.
No prior audiogram exists for comparison, making 'sudden' hard to confirm from a single visit → use the history (rate of symptom onset) as an equally valid trigger per the BAA definition.
Same-day referral pathways differ between weekday and weekend clinics → check both separately.
Small numbers make a single missed case dominate → review each miss individually as a case review, not just a percentage.
The urgent referral pathway exists on paper but the phone number is out of date → test the pathway before cycle 1 begins.
pearls: Recruit a hearing aid audiologist and an ENT consultant together, since the fix crosses both services.
Use existing audiogram comparison software, if available, to flag a sudden drop automatically at the point of testing.
Share the BAA definition as a laminated quick-reference card in each audiology test room.
Track time from same-day referral to first ENT contact as a natural follow-on audit.
effort: ~20 min per identified case from audiology and referral records
pass: Where the audiogram and history meet the BAA definition of sudden or rapid hearing loss, the audiology record shows a same-day referral for urgent medical assessment (ENT or emergency department), not a routine hearing aid pathway appointment.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of adults referred to a hearing aid service with confirmed sensorineural hearing loss suitable for amplification are fitted with their first hearing aid within 18 weeks of referral?
why: No audit of hearing aid fitting waiting times exists in the library, even though prolonged waits are a recognised access issue and the routine adult hearing aid pathway is explicitly funded to provide this service.

standard.source: Local standard, informed by the NHS Constitution 18-week referral-to-treatment standard and British Academy of Audiology description of the routine adult hearing aid pathway
standard.wording: Local standard: adults referred into the routine, direct-referral adult hearing aid pathway who are assessed as suitable for amplification should have their first hearing aid fitted within 18 weeks of referral, in line with the NHS referral-to-treatment standard, since (as the British Academy of Audiology notes) 'Routine, direct referral adult care pathways in the UK specifically fund hearing aid fitting'.
