population: Inclusion: adults referred to the routine adult hearing aid pathway, assessed and found suitable for amplification, over the sample period. Exclusion: patients identified as non-routine/complex under BAA criteria (audited separately) and those who decline or delay fitting by choice.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients who completed fitting in the last 3 months, from the audiology patient administration system.
data_source: Audiology patient administration system referral and fitting dates.
change: Introduce a 'straight to fit' pathway for straightforward, symmetrical age-related hearing loss, combining assessment and fitting in a single appointment where clinically appropriate, to reduce the number of separate visits driving the wait.
close_loop: Present at the audiology service and commissioner quality meeting; if achieved, embed the combined assessment-and-fit appointment as the default booking template.
evidence: No hearing aid fitting waiting-time audit exists in the library
pitfalls: Patients who decline an offered earlier appointment are wrongly counted as breaches → record patient-choice delays separately from service delays.
Hearing aid stock shortages for a particular model cause a spike in delays → track stock-related delays as a distinct reason code.
Complex or non-routine cases referred on to ENT are wrongly included, understating true routine-pathway performance → apply the exclusion consistently.
Waiting list data quality varies between clinics using different booking systems → validate a sample manually where systems differ.
Gains fade once waiting lists grow again after a temporary staffing boost → track the wait as a rolling monthly metric, not a one-off snapshot.
pearls: Recruit the audiology service manager and a senior hearing aid audiologist as co-authors.
Use the 'straight to fit' pathway pilot data to make a business case for wider rollout if it shortens waits without compromising quality.
Report waiting times alongside patient-reported outcome measures (for example hearing aid use at 3 months) to show waits are not just a numbers exercise.
Share results with commissioners, since hearing aid waiting times are often a locally monitored access metric.
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from the audiology patient administration system
pass: The audiology record shows the date of first hearing aid fitting within 18 weeks of the original referral date, for patients assessed as routine and suitable for amplification.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of females aged 12 to 55 attending the general (non-obstetric, non-orthopaedic-theatre) radiology department for a CT or fluoroscopic examination have a documented pregnancy status enquiry before the exposure?
why: No audit of pregnancy enquiry for general outpatient and inpatient radiology attendances exists in the library; existing entries cover orthopaedic theatre fluoroscopy and emergency surgical admissions, not the general radiology department pathway.

standard.source: Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017, regulation 11(1)(f)
standard.wording: A person must not carry out an exposure unless... in the case of an individual of childbearing potential, the person has enquired whether that individual is pregnant or breastfeeding, if relevant.

population: Inclusion: all females aged 12-55 attending general radiology (X-ray, CT, fluoroscopy) as outpatients or inpatients over the sample period. Exclusion: obstetric ultrasound and orthopaedic theatre exposures (audited under separate department-specific pathways).
sample: 40 consecutive eligible attendances over the last month, from the RIS.
data_source: RIS pre-exposure checklist, radiographer's exposure record.
change: Add a mandatory pregnancy-status field to the RIS pre-exposure checklist for all females aged 12-55, which the radiographer must complete before the exposure can be recorded as performed.
close_loop: Present at the radiology governance meeting; keep the mandatory RIS field permanently if the target is sustained, and include it in the department's written employer's procedures under IR(ME)R regulation 6.
evidence: No general radiology department pregnancy-enquiry audit exists in the library; related work covers orthopaedic theatre fluoroscopy (a proposed audit) and pregnancy testing in emergency surgical admissions [7712][6008]
pitfalls: Reception staff, not radiographers, ask the question and it is not passed on → clarify in the written procedure who is responsible and where it must be recorded.
The question is skipped for 'obviously' post-menopausal-looking patients → apply the age-band policy strictly regardless of appearance.
Urgent inpatient and out-of-hours exposures bypass the outpatient checklist → build the same mandatory field into the inpatient/urgent request workflow.
Patients decline to answer and this is recorded as 'not pregnant' by default → give 'declined to answer' as its own option requiring an escalation to the practitioner.
Gains fade after a RIS upgrade resets the field to optional → re-check after every system change.
pearls: Recruit the radiology superintendent radiographer and radiation protection supervisor together.
Use the RIS audit trail to pull data quickly rather than manual note review.
Cross-check the CT/fluoroscopy subgroup separately from plain film, since the fetal dose stakes differ.
Present this alongside the department's IR(ME)R regulation 7 clinical audit programme so it counts towards the statutory requirement.
effort: ~10 min per 10 attendances from the RIS
pass: A dated entry, made by the radiographer or radiology reception before the exposure, records that the patient was asked whether she is or might be pregnant, with the answer given.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of CT and MRI requests from general medical and surgical wards (excluding fracture clinic, already audited separately) state a specific clinical question that the imaging is expected to answer?
why: No audit of referrer information quality for general ward CT/MRI requests exists in the library; the corpus contains a related audit for fracture clinic X-ray requests only.

standard.source: Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017, regulation 10(5)
standard.wording: The referrer must supply the practitioner with sufficient medical data (such as previous diagnostic information or medical records) relevant to the exposure requested by the referrer to enable the practitioner to decide whether there is a sufficient net benefit as required by regulation 11(1)(b).

population: Inclusion: all CT and MRI requests from general adult medical and surgical inpatient wards over the sample period. Exclusion: fracture clinic and orthopaedic theatre requests (covered elsewhere), emergency department requests (a distinct high-volume pathway).
sample: 40 consecutive requests over the last 2 weeks, from the RIS.
data_source: RIS request record, vetting comments.
change: Make a free-text 'clinical question this scan should answer' field mandatory on the electronic CT/MRI request form, separate from the diagnosis field, so vetting radiologists can justify the request without chasing the ward.
close_loop: Present at the radiology and medical/surgical directorate joint governance meeting; keep the mandatory field if it reduces vetting queries.
evidence: No general ward CT/MRI clinical-question audit exists in the library; the corpus's comparable fracture clinic X-ray request audit uses the same IR(ME)R regulation 10(5) standard
pitfalls: Requesters paste the working diagnosis into the clinical question field without a real question → sample-check for genuine, specific questions versus copied diagnoses.
Junior doctors under time pressure default to brief text → pair the mandatory field with a short example bank of good clinical questions.
Vetting practitioners approve requests anyway despite a vague question, masking the true problem → track the proportion of requests returned for more information as a balancing measure.
The field becomes a free-text box that is easy to leave blank if the system allows it → make it a genuine hard stop, not just a labelled box.
Out-of-hours or verbal requests bypass the electronic form → include a parallel requirement for the on-call radiologist to document the clinical question when accepting a verbal request.
pearls: Recruit a vetting radiologist and a ward-based junior doctor educational lead.
Use the RIS audit trail to identify requests quickly rather than manual chart review.
Publish a one-page 'how to write a good imaging request' guide alongside the change.
Track vetting turnaround time as a related outcome measure, since clear requests should be justified faster.
effort: ~10 min per 10 requests from the RIS
pass: The electronic request includes a specific clinical question or working diagnosis (not just a test name), sufficient for the vetting practitioner to make a justification decision without contacting the referrer.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: For nasogastric tubes checked by X-ray because pH testing failed or aspirate could not be obtained, what proportion have documentation confirming the X-ray viewed was the correct, most current image for that patient, how the tube position was interpreted, and the resulting decision on feeding, recorded before any feed or medication was given?
why: No audit of the specific NPSA/2011/PSA002 documentation requirements for X-ray-confirmed nasogastric tube position exists in the library, distinct from the corpus's existing sticker-completion audit which does not test all three documentation elements together against the original alert wording.

standard.source: National Patient Safety Agency, Patient Safety Alert NPSA/2011/PSA002, Reducing the risk of harm caused by misplaced nasogastric feeding tubes in adults, children and infants (10 March 2011)
standard.wording: Documentation of the tube placement checking process includes confirmation that any x-ray viewed was the most current x-ray for the correct patient, how placement was interpreted, and clear instructions as to required actions. Any tubes identified to be in the lung are removed immediately, whether in the x-ray department or clinical area.

population: Inclusion: all adult inpatients whose nasogastric tube position was confirmed by X-ray (as a second-line test after pH testing failed or no aspirate was obtained) over the sample period. Exclusion: tubes confirmed by pH testing alone.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible X-ray-confirmed tube placements over the last 2-3 months, from radiology and ward records.
data_source: NG tube bedside documentation chart, radiology report, ward nursing notes.
change: Redesign the NG tube bedside chart so the three documentation elements (correct/current X-ray confirmed, interpretation, feeding decision) are a single mandatory sequence that must be completed and signed by a competency-assessed individual before the 'feed commenced' box can be ticked.
close_loop: Present at the trust patient safety/never events group, since misplaced NG tube feeding remains a Never Event category; keep the redesigned chart as the trust standard if the target is met.
evidence: [2329] closed-loop audit of NGT documentation using a sticker: sticker use 42.1% to 85%, position documented 63.1% to 75%, confirming staff recorded 60.5% to 75% after teaching and posters
[5472] avoiding never events in nasogastric intubation: interpretation errors fell from 7 to 1 and documentation improved by 22% after a mixed intervention
pitfalls: A sticker or chart is used but not fully completed, as shown in the corpus's own re-audit plateauing at 75-85% rather than 100% [2329] → require full completion, not partial, as the pass criterion.
Out-of-hours or agency staff are not trained in the competency framework → include NG tube X-ray interpretation competency in mandatory induction for all temporary staff.
The X-ray report and the bedside chart are completed by different people who do not cross-check each other → require the bedside documenter to state which X-ray (date/time) they reviewed.
Gains plateau rather than reach 100%, as seen in comparable audits [2329] → treat any gap as a live risk requiring a further PDSA cycle, not a finished project.
Feeding is started based on a verbal 'it looks fine' from radiology without full documentation → make the written record, not a verbal assurance, the requirement.
pearls: Recruit a ward sister, a radiographer/radiologist and the trust's patient safety lead together, since the corpus shows a mixed intervention (documentation, training and radiology involvement) works best [5472].
Use the trust's Never Events log as an early-warning cross-check for missed cases.
Reference the free e-learning tool for X-ray interpretation (as recommended in the alert) in staff training.
Report the audit at the same governance forum that reviews Never Events, to keep visibility high.
effort: ~15 min per case from NG tube charts and radiology reports
pass: The notes or NG tube chart record, before any feed or medication is given: confirmation the X-ray viewed was the current image for the correct patient, the interpreted position, and the resulting feeding decision, all signed and timed by a person assessed as competent.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of individuals involved in checking and interpreting nasogastric tube X-rays for feeding tube position have documented evidence of the competency assessment required by the national patient safety alert?
why: No audit of staff competency assessment (as opposed to the clinical documentation itself) for NG tube X-ray interpretation exists in the library; this is the underlying systems failure identified as the main cause of harm in the national alert.

standard.source: National Patient Safety Agency, Patient Safety Alert NPSA/2011/PSA002 (10 March 2011)
standard.wording: Any individual involved with nasogastric tube position checks has been assessed as competent through theoretical and practical learning... Staff training, competency frameworks and supervision are reviewed to ensure that all healthcare professionals involved with nasogastric tube position checks have been assessed as competent. Competency training should include theoretical and practical learning.

population: Inclusion: all staff (doctors, nurses, advanced clinical practitioners) whose name appears as the interpreter on NG tube position documentation over the sample period. Exclusion: none.
sample: 30 named staff identified from NG tube charts over the last 3 months, cross-checked against the trust training record system.
data_source: NG tube bedside chart (interpreter name), trust learning management/training record system.
change: Restrict access to record an NG tube X-ray interpretation on the electronic chart to staff whose training record system shows an in-date competency assessment, using a role-based system permission rather than relying on self-declaration.
close_loop: Present at the trust patient safety/never events group; keep the system-level permission restriction if it is deliverable and the target is met.
evidence: [5472] avoiding never events in nasogastric intubation practice: interpretation errors fell from 7 to 1 after a mixed intervention that included interpretation training
pitfalls: Staff interpret tube position without being named formally, so the chart undercounts who is actually doing the checking → cross-reference ward rota data as a sanity check.
Competency assessments lapse without a renewal reminder → set an automatic expiry alert in the training record system.
Locum and agency staff are excluded from the trust's own training record system → agree an equivalent competency-verification process for temporary staff before their first shift.
The audit is seen as a training-department task rather than a clinical safety issue → present findings jointly with the patient safety team, not training alone.
A system-level access restriction is technically difficult and gets delayed indefinitely → set an interim manual sign-off process while the system change is built.
pearls: Recruit the trust's practice development nurse or education lead as co-author.
Use the existing electronic learning management system's reporting function to pull competency data quickly.
Combine this with the documentation-quality audit above, using the same case sample, to save data collection time.
Report the proportion of NG tube-competent staff per ward as a workforce planning metric, not just a compliance figure.
effort: ~10 min per 10 staff records from the training system
pass: The staff member's training record shows a completed, in-date competency assessment (theoretical and practical) for nasogastric tube X-ray interpretation, matched against the name recorded on the NG tube documentation.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of accidental or unintended radiation exposures identified by the imaging department are reported to the employer's radiation protection lead within the timeframe set out in the trust's IR(ME)R accidental exposure procedure?
why: No audit of accidental/unintended exposure reporting timeliness exists in the library, despite this being a specific, named employer duty under IR(ME)R with its own regulation.

standard.source: Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017, regulation 8 (Employer's duties: accidental or unintended exposure)
standard.wording: Regulation 8: Employer's duties: accidental or unintended exposure.

population: Inclusion: all incidents identified by radiology or nuclear medicine staff as an accidental or unintended exposure over the audit period (e.g. wrong patient, wrong side, wrong protocol, repeat exposure). Exclusion: near misses caught before exposure occurred (may be tracked separately).
sample: All identified incidents over the last 6-12 months (expect a small number in most departments), from the Datix/incident reporting system and radiation protection log.
data_source: Datix or equivalent incident reporting system, radiation protection adviser's log.
change: Add a mandatory 'radiation incident' category to the Datix incident form that automatically emails the radiation protection lead at the point of submission, removing the dependency on staff remembering a separate manual notification step.
close_loop: Present at the radiation protection committee, which has a statutory duty to review such incidents; keep the automatic Datix routing if the target is sustained.
evidence: No accidental/unintended exposure reporting-timeliness audit exists in the library
pitfalls: Staff under-report minor errors for fear of blame → frame the audit and any feedback around system learning, not individual blame, from the outset.
Incidents are logged on Datix under a generic category and are hard to find → create a specific radiation-incident category before cycle 1.
Small numbers make the percentage very sensitive to a single case → review every case individually as well as reporting the overall rate.
Reporting requirements to the enforcing authority (for notifiable incidents) are confused with internal reporting → keep the two steps separate in the template.
Gains fade if the automatic email routing is not tested after a Datix system upgrade → re-verify after any system change.
pearls: Recruit the radiation protection adviser and radiation protection supervisor as co-authors; this is their statutory area.
Use existing Datix reports as the primary data source rather than building a new log.
Report trends in error type (not just reporting timeliness) to help target future dose-reduction work.
Present this as a standing item at the radiation protection committee, which already meets on a fixed schedule to review such incidents.
effort: ~20 min per incident from Datix and the radiation protection log
pass: Every identified accidental or unintended exposure incident is reported to the employer's radiation protection lead (and, where required, onward to the enforcing authority) within the timeframe set out in the trust's own written IR(ME)R regulation 8 procedure.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of adult CT pulmonary angiogram examinations for suspected pulmonary embolism have a dose-length product at or below the national diagnostic reference level for that examination?
why: No audit of CT pulmonary angiogram dose optimisation against the national diagnostic reference level exists in the library; a comparable audit exists for CT head in suspected stroke, but CTPA is a distinct high-volume examination with its own reference level.

standard.source: Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017, regulation 12(3)(c) (Optimisation); UKHSA National Diagnostic Reference Levels
standard.wording: Regulation 12(3)(c) requires the employer to establish diagnostic reference levels for standard radiodiagnostic examinations and to ensure they are used as part of the optimisation of exposures; UKHSA publishes the National Diagnostic Reference Levels used to benchmark local practice.

population: Inclusion: all adult CTPA examinations performed for suspected pulmonary embolism over the sample period on each scanner. Exclusion: paediatric examinations and CTPA performed for other indications (e.g. pre-procedural planning) where a different protocol may apply.
sample: 20 consecutive examinations per scanner over the last month, from the CT dose-recording system.
data_source: CT scanner dose report (DLP), medical physics expert's dose audit records.
change: Review the CTPA scan protocol on each scanner with the medical physics expert (tube current modulation, scan range, iterative reconstruction settings) and lock the optimised protocol so individual radiographers cannot alter key dose-determining parameters.
target: Median dose-length product at or below the national diagnostic reference level
reaudit: At 6 months, same scanners and sample size.
close_loop: Present at the radiation protection committee and imaging governance meeting; if achieved, extend the locked-protocol approach to other high-volume CT examinations.
evidence: No CTPA-specific diagnostic reference level audit exists in the library; a related proposed audit covers CT head dose in suspected stroke against the national diagnostic reference level
pitfalls: Scan range is extended unnecessarily beyond the chest, inflating dose without diagnostic benefit → check scan range against the protocol as a specific data point, not just overall dose.
Obese or very large patients are compared against the same reference level without size adjustment → report by weight band, since diagnostic reference levels are typically set for a standard adult.
A single scanner with an outdated protocol skews the trust-wide average → report per scanner, not just an overall trust figure.
The medical physics expert review takes months to complete → set an interim manual check while the formal review is under way.
Gains fade after a software or protocol upgrade resets settings → re-verify dose data after any scanner software update.
pearls: Recruit the medical physics expert and CT superintendent radiographer as joint leads.
Use the scanner's automatic dose-recording software to pull data quickly rather than manual review of each study.
Compare results across all CT scanners in the department to identify and share best practice from the lowest-dose scanner.
Report dose trends over time on a simple run chart at the radiation protection committee.
effort: ~10 min per 10 examinations from the CT dose-recording system
pass: The median dose-length product for the audited sample of adult CTPA examinations is at or below the current UKHSA national diagnostic reference level for CT pulmonary angiography.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of diagnostic imaging examinations using ionising radiation are covered by the employer's written procedures required under IR(ME)R, and what proportion of these procedures have been reviewed within the last 3 years?
why: No audit of the completeness and currency of the employer's written IR(ME)R procedures exists in the library, even though these procedures are the legal foundation for every other radiation-safety check in the department.

standard.source: Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017, regulation 6 (Employer's duties: establishment of general procedures, protocols and quality assurance programmes)
standard.wording: Regulation 6: Employer's duties: establishment of general procedures, protocols and quality assurance programmes.

population: Inclusion: all distinct examination types listed in the department's examination protocol library. Exclusion: none.
sample: All examination types held in the department's protocol library, cross-checked against the procedure document register.
data_source: Department procedure/protocol document register, quality management system.
change: Build a single procedure register with an automatic 3-year review reminder sent to the named clinical lead for each examination type, replacing any informal or undated local protocol sheets.
close_loop: Present at the radiation protection committee and quality management system review meeting; keep the automatic review reminder as a permanent governance control.
evidence: No audit of IR(ME)R employer's procedure completeness or currency exists in the library
pitfalls: Procedures exist informally (in a folder or on a noticeboard) but are not in the formal register → treat any procedure not in the register as absent for this audit's purposes.
Reviewed procedures are re-approved without any real content change, giving false reassurance → sample-check a subset for evidence of genuine review, not just a new date stamp.

New examination types (e.g. a newly introduced protocol) are added to clinical use before the written procedure exists → require sign-off from the procedure register before any new protocol goes live.
The review reminder system is not monitored, so overdue procedures accumulate silently → assign a named individual to review the register monthly.
Different sites within a multi-site trust hold different versions of the same procedure → check consistency across sites as part of the audit.
pearls: Recruit the imaging quality manager and radiation protection supervisor together, since this underpins the department's Care Quality Commission-equivalent governance evidence.
Use this audit as an opportunity to consolidate any duplicate or conflicting procedure documents found across sites.
Link the register to the department's ISO/IQIPS accreditation evidence, since procedure currency is typically already assessed there.
Report the audit findings to the trust's overarching radiation protection committee, since this is a standing legal requirement, not a one-off improvement project.
effort: ~30 min reviewing the procedure register against the protocol library
pass: Each distinct type of examination performed in the department (by modality and, where relevant, by clinical indication) is covered by a current written employer's procedure, reviewed and re-approved within the last 3 years.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: What proportion of interventional radiology procedures carried out under fluoroscopic or CT guidance have the total dose-area product or dose-length product for the procedure documented in the patient record?
why: No audit of interventional radiology procedure dose documentation (as distinct from diagnostic CT dose optimisation) exists in the library, despite interventional procedures often delivering the highest doses in a department.

standard.source: Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations 2017, Schedule 2, paragraph 1(j)
standard.wording: Schedule 2 sets out the data to be recorded for each exposure, including the radiation dose delivered, which for interventional procedures includes the dose-area product or equivalent dose metric for the procedure.

population: Inclusion: all interventional radiology procedures using fluoroscopic or CT guidance over the sample period. Exclusion: diagnostic-only fluoroscopy studies (e.g. barium studies) without an interventional component.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible procedures over the last 2-3 months, from the interventional radiology procedure log.
data_source: Interventional radiology procedure note, RIS/dose-tracking system.
change: Configure the interventional radiology system to automatically populate the total procedure dose into the electronic procedure note at the point the procedure is closed, removing reliance on manual transcription.
close_loop: Present at the interventional radiology and radiation protection joint governance meeting; keep the automatic dose transfer if the target is met.
evidence: No interventional radiology procedure dose-documentation audit exists in the library; a related proposed audit covers trauma theatre fluoroscopy dose recording in the operation note
pitfalls: Long or complex procedures with multiple fluoroscopy runs have the dose recorded only for the final run, understating the true total → confirm the figure used is the cumulative procedure total, not a single exposure.
Manual transcription from the fluoroscopy unit display to the notes introduces transcription errors → prefer automatic electronic transfer wherever the system allows it.

Skin-dose alert thresholds are confused with the routine dose-documentation requirement → keep this audit focused on documentation completeness, with skin-dose alerts as a separate, higher-threshold safety check.
Complex cases performed by visiting or locum interventionalists are more likely to have incomplete documentation → include this explicitly in visiting-practitioner induction.
Gains fade if the automatic transfer is not tested after an equipment software update → re-verify after any upgrade.
pearls: Recruit the interventional radiology lead and radiation protection adviser together.
Use this audit to also identify any procedures approaching or exceeding local skin-dose alert thresholds, as a valuable by-product.
Report dose trends by procedure type to support future protocol optimisation work.
Present alongside the department's regulation 13 population dose estimate work, since procedure-level data feeds that wider requirement.
effort: ~10 min per 10 procedures from the procedure log
pass: The patient record (procedure note, RIS record or electronic dose report) documents the total dose-area product (fluoroscopy) or dose-length product (CT-guided) for the completed interventional procedure.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
question: For planned (non-emergency) interventional radiology procedures, what proportion of patients have their informed consent confirmed at a separate discussion with the radiologist actually performing the procedure, distinct from the initial information-giving discussion?
why: No audit of this specific two-stage consent process for interventional radiology exists in the library; the corpus's extensive consent-documentation topic focuses on written risk completeness on consent forms generally, not this process step unique to radiology.

standard.source: Royal College of Radiologists, Standards for patient consent particular to radiology, second edition
standard.wording: Interventional or invasive radiological procedures require particular attention in obtaining the express consent of the patient. In a planned procedure, the patient should receive information, verbally or in writing, in sufficient time before the procedure to consider it and to consult others if they so wish. The patient should have their informed consent confirmed at a separate discussion with the radiologist performing the procedure.

population: Inclusion: all planned (non-emergency) interventional radiology procedures over the sample period. Exclusion: emergency, unplanned procedures where the standard explicitly allows clinical judgement on timing.
sample: 40 consecutive planned procedures over the last 2-3 months, from the interventional radiology booking system.
data_source: Pre-procedure clinic letter or information-giving record, procedure day consent confirmation note.
change: Add a mandatory 'consent confirmed by performing radiologist' field, with date, time and location, to the interventional radiology electronic procedure record, separate from the initial information-giving documentation.
close_loop: Present at the interventional radiology governance meeting; keep the mandatory field permanently if the target is met.
evidence: The corpus's consent-documentation topic card describes this area as heavily over-audited for generic risk completeness (45 audits) but notes that whether consent starts in clinic rather than on the day is one of the under-explored angles the consultant advice recommends auditing instead
pitfalls: The 'separate discussion' happens in the procedure room immediately before sedation, which the standard specifically discourages → record the physical location, not just that a discussion happened.
Same-day add-on cases blur the distinction between initial information and confirmation → apply the emergency/unplanned exclusion strictly rather than stretching it to cover convenience add-ons.
A generic consent form is signed without evidence of a genuine second discussion → look for narrative evidence of the discussion, not just a signature.

Patients seen only briefly by a different radiologist than the one performing the procedure may not meet the standard's intent → record whether the confirming radiologist was the same person who performed the procedure.
Gains fade once the mandatory field becomes a box ticked without a real discussion → spot-check a sample against patient-reported experience where feasible.
pearls: Recruit the interventional radiology lead and a specialist nurse who runs pre-procedure clinics.
Use existing pre-assessment clinic letters as the source for the 'initial information' half of the audit.
Present findings alongside patient experience feedback on how well-prepared they felt for the procedure.
Keep this as a standing item in the interventional radiology multidisciplinary team meeting, not just a one-off project.
effort: ~15 min per 10 procedures from booking and consent records
pass: The notes record two distinct consent-related contacts: an initial information-giving discussion in advance of the procedure, and a separate confirmation of consent with the performing radiologist, both documented with dates.

question: What proportion of interventional radiology procedures classified locally as complex or carrying significant risk have written consent (a signed consent form), rather than verbal consent alone, documented before the procedure?
why: No audit specifically of the written-versus-verbal consent threshold for complex interventional radiology procedures exists in the library, separate from the general consent-completeness topic already heavily covered for surgical specialties.

standard.source: Royal College of Radiologists, Standards for patient consent particular to radiology, second edition, citing General Medical Council guidance
standard.wording: The General Medical Council (GMC) suggests that written consent should be taken in cases where: the treatment or procedure is complex and involves significant risk and/or side-effects... With planned procedures, consideration should be given to asking the patient to sign a written consent form for those examinations and procedures which are recognised to be more complex to undertake or which potentially carry a more serious risk of complication.

population: Inclusion: all interventional radiology procedures on the department's agreed complex/significant-risk list over the sample period. Exclusion: procedures not on the list, where verbal consent with a documented discussion may be sufficient.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible procedures over the last 2-3 months, from the interventional radiology log.
data_source: Interventional radiology procedure log, consent form archive.
change: Publish an agreed department list of procedures requiring written consent (built from the GMC/RCR criteria) and introduce procedure-specific consent forms for the highest-volume complex procedures, since the corpus shows procedure-specific forms are the fix that reliably works for consent completeness.
reaudit: At 4 months, same list and sample size.
close_loop: Present at the interventional radiology governance meeting; keep the published list and procedure-specific forms if the target is met.
evidence: The corpus's consent-documentation topic card reports that pre-printed or procedure-specific consent forms reach close to 100% completeness of documented risks, compared with teaching alone which gives only partial gains
pitfalls: Staff disagree on which procedures count as 'complex' without a published list → agree and publish the list with radiology leadership before cycle 1.
A generic hospital consent form is used instead of a procedure-specific one, missing procedure-relevant risks → track use of the correct, procedure-specific form as a separate data point.
Verbal consent is documented in detail but no form is signed, technically failing the standard despite good practice → count only signed forms as meeting 'written consent' for this audit.
Emergency conversions from a planned to an urgent procedure blur the consent pathway → record these separately rather than excluding them silently.
Gains plateau below 100% once the list is published but not enforced → build the list into the booking system so a procedure on it cannot be booked without a linked consent form.
pearls: Recruit the interventional radiology lead and a specialist nurse or consent lead as co-authors.
Reuse procedure-specific consent form templates from surgical specialties as a starting point where suitable.
Present the audit alongside the corpus's own consent-documentation learning (procedure-specific forms work; teaching alone does not) to justify the chosen fix.
Track patient understanding of risks as a longer-term follow-on measure once form completeness is achieved.
effort: ~10 min per 10 procedures from the consent form archive
pass: For every procedure on the department's locally agreed 'complex/significant risk' list, a signed written consent form is present in the record before the procedure starts.

question: What proportion of interventional radiology procedures have a completed Sign In, Time Out and Sign Out safety checklist, adapted from the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist for radiological interventions, on file before, during and after the procedure?
why: No audit of WHO-style checklist completion specifically for interventional radiology procedures exists in the library, distinct from the theatre-based WHO checklist audits already covered for surgical specialties.

standard.source: Royal College of Radiologists, WHO Surgical Safety Checklist: for Radiological Interventions Only (adapted from the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist)
standard.wording: The Royal College of Radiologists adapted the checklist of Safe Surgery from the World Health Organization for use in radiological interventions in England and Wales, entitled 'WHO Surgical Safety Checklist: for Radiological Interventions ONLY', with the three phases of Sign In, Team Time Out and Sign Out.

population: Inclusion: all interventional radiology procedures performed in the interventional suite over the sample period. Exclusion: bedside procedures performed outside the interventional suite (audited under a separate ward-based safety process).
sample: 40 consecutive procedures over the last month, from the interventional radiology log.
data_source: Interventional radiology WHO checklist form, procedure log.
change: Designate a named 'checklist champion' for each interventional radiology session, responsible for leading and confirming all three checklist phases out loud, with the checklist itself made a mandatory field in the electronic procedure record rather than a paper form that can be left incomplete.
close_loop: Present at the interventional radiology and theatre safety governance meeting; keep the checklist champion role and electronic mandatory field if the target is met.
evidence: No interventional radiology-specific WHO checklist completion audit exists in the library
pitfalls: The checklist is completed retrospectively rather than in real time, defeating its safety purpose → spot-check timing against the procedure start time where the electronic system logs it.
Staff view the checklist as a barrier for 'quick' procedures and skip it → apply it to all procedures on the interventional list regardless of expected duration.
A paper checklist is easily lost or left blank → prefer an electronic mandatory field that blocks progression to the next step.

The general anaesthetic section, largely irrelevant to most interventional cases, causes staff to disengage with the whole checklist → confirm the department is using the RCR-adapted version, not the unmodified surgical version.
Champions rotate without a clear handover, and the role lapses → build champion allocation into the weekly interventional list planning.
pearls: Recruit an interventional radiology consultant and the lead interventional radiology nurse/radiographer together.
Designate a champion for each list as recommended in published implementation experience with this checklist.
Use a clipboard or fixed location for the checklist so it is always available at the point of use.
Report near-miss catches attributed to the checklist (e.g. wrong side identified at Time Out) as a powerful qualitative measure alongside completion rates.
effort: ~10 min per 10 procedures from the checklist archive
pass: All three phases of the checklist (Sign In, Time Out, Sign Out) are completed and filed in the procedure record for the case.

question: What proportion of patients undergoing an intimate radiological examination or procedure (for example transrectal or transvaginal procedures) have express consent and the offer of a chaperone documented before the examination?
why: No audit of chaperone offer and express consent documentation for intimate radiological examinations exists in the library.

standard.source: Royal College of Radiologists, Standards for patient consent particular to radiology, second edition
standard.wording: Intimate examinations require particular attention and understanding to establish trust and mutual confidence between patient and doctor... Express consent, either verbally or in writing, should be obtained for intimate examinations and serious consideration should be given to the need to provide a chaperone.

population: Inclusion: all patients having an intimate radiological examination or procedure (e.g. transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsy, transvaginal ultrasound where performed by radiology) over the sample period. Exclusion: none.
sample: 30-40 consecutive eligible examinations over the last 2-3 months, from the department booking system.
data_source: Procedure note, department booking/checklist record.
change: Add a mandatory 'chaperone offered: outcome' field, alongside the express consent field, to the booking or procedure checklist for all examinations coded as intimate, so the step cannot be skipped or forgotten.
close_loop: Present at the department governance meeting; keep the mandatory field if the target is met.
evidence: No chaperone/express-consent documentation audit for intimate radiological examinations exists in the library
pitfalls: Staff assume a chaperone is 'obviously' not needed for certain examinations and skip documenting the offer → require the field to be completed for every examination on the intimate-examination list, with 'not applicable' as an explicit, reasoned option rather than a blank.
Patients decline a chaperone and this is not distinguished from 'not offered' → give both options explicitly in the template.
Locum or visiting staff are unaware which examinations are classified as intimate locally → publish and circulate the local list.
The field exists on paper but not in the electronic system used for most bookings → prioritise adding it to whichever system captures the majority of these examinations.
Gains are not sustained after a staff rotation → include the requirement in departmental induction for new radiographers, sonographers and radiologists.
pearls: Recruit a radiographer or sonographer who regularly performs these examinations as co-author.
Publish a simple, agreed list of which examinations count as 'intimate' locally to reduce ambiguity.
Present alongside patient experience feedback, since chaperone offer is a well-recognised patient dignity marker.
Keep the audit brief and focused, since this is a quick, high-value dignity-of-care check rather than a complex clinical audit.
effort: ~10 min per 10 examinations from booking records
pass: The record shows express consent obtained (verbally or in writing) and documented consideration of a chaperone (offered and accepted, offered and declined, or not applicable with reason) before the examination.
